title: IV. The Confession Of A Passionate Heart—In Anecdote
paragraphs: “I was living wildly in those days. Father said just now that I spent several thousand roubles on seducing young girls. That’s a filthy invention. Nothing of the sort happened. And if it did, I didn’t need money for _that_. For me, money is a trimming, the overflow of my heart, the frame. One day she’d be my lady; the next, some girl from the street would be in her place. I entertained them both. I tossed money away by the fistful on music, wild parties and gypsies. Sometimes I handed it to the ladies too, since they grab it eagerly, I have to admit, and are pleased and thankful for it. Ladies were fond of me. Not every one, but it happened, it happened. Still, I always preferred the side-paths, the little dark back-alleys off the main road. That’s where the adventures are, and the surprises, and the precious metal in the dirt. I’m talking figuratively, brother. The town I lived in had no back-alleys like that in the literal sense, but morally it had plenty. If you were like me, you’d know what I mean. I loved vice. I loved the disgrace of vice. I loved cruelty. Am I not a bug, a noxious insect? A Karamazov, in a word! Once a whole crowd of us drove out on a picnic, in seven sledges. It was winter and dark, and I began squeezing a girl’s hand and forced her to kiss me. She was the daughter of an official, a sweet, gentle, yielding creature. She let me, she let me do a great deal in the dark. She thought, poor thing, that I’d come the next day and propose. (I was thought a good catch, too.) But for five months I didn’t say one word to her. At dances (we had dances all the time) I would see her in a corner with her eyes on me. I saw them glow with a fire, a fire of gentle indignation. This game just tickled the insect lust I kept in my soul. Five months later she married an official and left town, still angry, and still, perhaps, in love with me. Now they’re happy together. Note that I told nobody. I didn’t brag about it. I’m full of low desires and I love what’s low, but I’m not dishonorable. You’re blushing; your eyes flashed. That’s enough of this filth with you. And all that was nothing much, wayside blossoms _à la_ Paul de Kock, though the cruel insect had already grown strong in my soul. I’ve a whole album of memories, brother. God bless them, the darlings. I always tried to part without a quarrel. And I never gave them away. I never bragged about even one. But enough of that. You can’t think I brought you here only to talk such nonsense. No. What I’m going to tell you is more curious. And don’t be surprised that I’m glad to tell it, instead of being ashamed.”
“You’re saying that because I blushed,” Alyosha said suddenly. “I didn’t blush at what you were telling me or at what you’ve done. I blushed because I’m just like you.”
“You? Oh, come on. That’s going a bit too far!”

“It isn’t too far,” said Alyosha warmly (plainly he had thought this before). “It’s the same ladder. I’m on the bottom step and you’re up above, around the thirteenth. That’s how I see it. But it comes to the same thing. It’s exactly the same kind of thing. Whoever is on the bottom step is bound to climb to the top one.”
“Then you shouldn’t step on the ladder at all.”
“Anyone who can avoid it had better not.”
“But can you?”
“I don’t think so.”

“Hush, Alyosha, hush, my dear! You touch me so much I could kiss your hand. That rogue Grushenka knows men. She told me once that she’d eat you up some day. There, there, I won’t go on! Let’s leave this field of rot, all over flies, and go on to my tragedy, which is also all over flies, meaning every kind of baseness. The old man lied when he said I seduced innocence. But my tragedy did have something like that in it, though it happened only once, and even then it didn’t come off. The old man who accuses me of what never happened doesn’t even know about this. I never told anybody. You’re the first, apart from Ivan, of course. Ivan knows everything. He knew it long before you did. But Ivan is a tomb.”
“Ivan is a tomb?”
“Yes.”
Alyosha listened with great attention.

“I was a lieutenant in a line regiment, but I was still watched, like a sort of convict. Even so, the little town received me awfully well. I spent money left and right. People took me for rich, and so did I. But I must have charmed them in other ways too. They shook their heads over me, yet they liked me. My colonel, an old man, suddenly took against me. He was forever picking on me. But I had powerful friends, and the whole town besides was on my side, so he couldn’t do me much harm. It was my own fault, for I wouldn’t show him proper respect. I was proud. This stubborn old fellow was really a very decent sort, kind-hearted and hospitable. He’d had two wives, and both were dead. His first wife, from a humble family, left a daughter as unpretentious as herself. When I was there she was a young woman of twenty-four. She lived with her father and an aunt, her mother’s sister. The aunt was simple and had no schooling; the niece was simple too, but lively. I like saying nice things about people. I never knew a woman with a more charming nature than Agafya. Imagine, her name was Agafya Ivanovna! And she wasn’t bad-looking either, in the Russian way: tall, stout, with a full figure and beautiful eyes, though her face was rather coarse. She’d never married, though two men had asked her. She said no to both and stayed as cheerful as ever. We were close, though not in ‘that’ way. It was pure friendship. I’ve often been friends with women quite innocently. I talked to her with shocking frankness, and she only laughed. Many women enjoy such freedom, and since she was a girl as well, it was very amusing. And another thing: you could never think of her as a young lady. She and her aunt lived in her father’s house with a kind of chosen humility, never setting themselves up as equal to other people. Everyone liked her and she was useful to all, being a clever dressmaker. She had a talent for it. She gave her work freely, asking for nothing, but if someone offered to pay, she didn’t say no. The colonel, of course, was another matter altogether. He was one of the leading figures of the district. He kept open house and entertained the whole town, with suppers and dances. When I arrived and joined the battalion, the whole town was talking about the colonel’s second daughter, a great beauty, who was expected home any day. She had just left a fashionable school in the capital. This second daughter is Katerina Ivanovna. She was the child of the second wife, who came from the family of a distinguished general. Though, as I learned on good authority, she too brought the colonel no money. She had connections, and that was all. There may have been expectations, but they had come to nothing.

“Still, when the young lady came home from boarding-school for a visit, the whole town woke up. Our most distinguished ladies took her up at once—two ‘Excellencies’ and a colonel’s wife—and everyone else followed their lead and gave parties in her honor. She was the belle of the balls and picnics, and they staged _tableaux vivants_ to help poor governesses. I paid no attention and went on as wildly as before. In fact, one of my exploits just then set the whole town talking. One evening at the battery commander’s I saw her eyes taking my measure. I didn’t go over to her, as if I scorned to know her. Soon after, at an evening party, I did go over and speak to her. She barely looked at me and pursed her lips in scorn. ‘Just wait. I’ll get even,’ I thought. I played the awful fool many times back then, and I knew it myself. What made it worse was that I could tell ‘Katenka’ was no innocent boarding-school miss but a person of character, proud and truly principled. Above all she had education and intellect, and I had neither. You think I meant to propose? No. I only wanted revenge, because I was such a hero and she didn’t seem to feel it.

“Meanwhile I passed my time in drink and riot, until the lieutenant-colonel put me under arrest for three days. Right then Father sent me six thousand roubles. In return I’d sent him a deed giving up all claims on him—settling our accounts, so to speak, and saying I’d expect nothing more. I didn’t understand a word of it then. Until I came here, Alyosha, until the last few days really, and maybe even now, I haven’t been able to make head or tail of my money affairs with Father. But never mind that. We’ll talk about it later.

“The moment I got the money, a letter came from a friend, telling me something that interested me enormously. The authorities, I learned, were unhappy with our lieutenant-colonel. He was suspected of irregularities. In fact, his enemies were preparing a surprise for him. Then the commander of the division arrived and kicked up the devil of a row. Soon afterwards the colonel was ordered to retire. I won’t tell you how it all happened. He certainly had enemies. All at once the town went markedly cold on him and his whole family. His friends all turned their backs. That was when I took my first step. I met Agafya Ivanovna, whom I’d always been friendly with, and said, ‘Do you know that 4,500 roubles of government money is missing from your father’s accounts?’
“‘What do you mean? Why do you say that? The general was here not long ago and everything was all right.’
“‘It was then. It isn’t now.’
“She was terribly frightened.
“‘Don’t scare me!’ she said. ‘Who told you that?’

“‘Don’t be alarmed,’ I said. ‘I won’t tell a soul. You know I’m silent as the grave. I only wanted to add, in case of “possibilities,” that when they demand the 4,500 roubles from your father and he can’t produce it, he’ll be tried and made to serve as a common soldier in his old age. Unless you’d like to send your young lady to me, secretly. I’ve just been paid some money. I’ll give her four thousand, if you like, and keep the secret religiously.’
“‘Oh, you scoundrel!’—those were her words. ‘You wicked scoundrel! How dare you!’

“She stormed off, furiously indignant, while I shouted after her once more that the secret would be kept sacred. I may as well say right away that those two simple creatures, Agafya and her aunt, behaved like perfect angels through this whole affair. They truly adored their ‘Katya.’ They thought her far above themselves and waited on her hand and foot. But Agafya told her about our conversation. I found that out later. She didn’t hold anything back, and of course that was all I wanted.

“Suddenly the new major arrived to take over the battalion. The old lieutenant-colonel fell ill at once. For two days he couldn’t leave his room, and he didn’t hand over the government money. Dr. Kravchenko declared he really was ill. But I knew for a fact, and had known for a long time, that for the past four years the money had never been in his hands except when the Commander came on inspection. He used to lend it to a man he could trust, a merchant of our town named Trifonov, an old widower with a big beard and gold-rimmed spectacles. Trifonov would go to the fair, make a profitable business out of the money, and return the whole sum to the colonel, along with a present from the fair and interest on the loan. This time, though (I heard all about it by pure chance from Trifonov’s son and heir, a slobbering youth and one of the most vicious in the world)—this time, I say, Trifonov brought nothing back from the fair. The lieutenant-colonel flew at him. ‘I’ve never had any money from you, and couldn’t possibly have had any.’ That was the only answer he got. So now our lieutenant-colonel sits shut up at home with a towel round his head, and all three of them are busy putting ice on it. Suddenly an orderly appears with the book and the order to ‘hand over the battalion money at once, within two hours.’ He signed the book (I saw the signature in it afterwards) and got up, saying he would put on his uniform. He ran to his bedroom, loaded his double-barreled gun with a service bullet, pulled the boot off his right foot, set the gun against his chest, and began feeling for the trigger with his toe. But Agafya, remembering what I’d told her, was suspicious. She crept up and looked into the room just in time. She rushed in, threw herself on him from behind and wrapped her arms round him. The gun went off, hit the ceiling and hurt no one. The others ran in, took the gun away and held him by the arms. I heard all this afterwards. I was at home. It was getting dark, and I was about to go out. I had dressed, brushed my hair, scented my handkerchief and picked up my cap, when suddenly the door opened, and in front of me in the room stood Katerina Ivanovna.

“Strange how things turn out sometimes. Nobody had seen her in the street, so nobody in the town knew. I lodged with two decrepit old ladies who looked after me. They were the most obliging old things and would do anything for me, and when I asked, they kept as quiet afterwards as two cast-iron posts. Of course I understood the situation at once. She came in and looked me straight in the face, her dark eyes determined, even defiant, but on her lips and around her mouth I saw uncertainty.
“‘My sister has told me,’ she began, ‘that you’ll give me 4,500 roubles if I come and ask you for it myself. I’ve come ... give me the money!’
“She couldn’t keep it up. She was out of breath and frightened, her voice gave out, and the corners of her mouth and the lines around it trembled. Alyosha, are you listening, or are you asleep?”
“Mitya, I know you’ll tell the whole truth,” said Alyosha, agitated.

“I am telling it. If I tell the whole truth just as it happened, I won’t spare myself. My first thought was a—Karamazov one. A centipede bit me once, brother, and I lay in bed with fever for a fortnight. Well, that’s how it felt then: a centipede biting at my heart—a noxious insect, you understand? I looked her over from head to foot. You’ve seen her? She’s a beauty. But she was beautiful in a different way then. At that moment she was beautiful because she was noble and I was a scoundrel. She stood there in all the grandeur of her generosity, sacrificing herself for her father, and I—a bug! Scoundrel that I was, she was entirely in my power, body and soul. She was cornered. I tell you frankly, that thought, that venomous thought, took such hold of my heart that it nearly fainted with suspense. It seemed there was no resisting it. I felt I would act like a bug, like a venomous spider, without a spark of pity. I could scarcely breathe. Understand me: I would have gone the next day to ask for her hand, so it might all end honorably, so to speak, and nobody would or could know. Because I may be a man of base desires, but I’m honest. And that very second some voice seemed to whisper in my ear, ‘But when you come tomorrow to propose, that girl won’t even see you. She’ll tell her coachman to throw you out of the yard. “Shout it all over town,” she’ll say. “I’m not afraid of you.”’ I looked at the young lady, and my voice hadn’t deceived me. That was exactly how it would be, no doubt of it. I could tell from her face that I’d be thrown out of the house. My spite was aroused. I wanted to play her the nastiest, most swinish cad’s trick there is: to look at her with a sneer, and right there where she stood in front of me, to stun her with a tone of voice only a shopman could use.

“‘Four thousand! What are you talking about? I was joking. You’ve counted your chickens too soon, madam. Two hundred, if you like, with all my heart. But four thousand is no sum to throw away on a frivolity like that. You’ve put yourself out for nothing.’

“Of course I’d have lost the game. She would have run away. But it would have been an infernal revenge, and worth everything. I’d have howled with regret the rest of my life, only for having played that trick. Would you believe it, with no other woman, not one, has it ever happened to me that I looked at her with hatred at such a moment. But I swear on my oath, for three seconds, or maybe five, I looked at her with a fearful hatred—the kind of hate that is only a hair’s-breadth from love, from the maddest love!

“I went to the window and pressed my forehead against the frozen pane, and I remember the ice burned my forehead like fire. I didn’t keep her long, don’t be afraid. I turned round, went to the table, opened the drawer and took out a banknote for five thousand roubles (it was lying in a French dictionary). I showed it to her without a word, folded it and handed it to her. I opened the door into the passage, stepped back and made her a deep bow, a most respectful, most impressive bow, believe me! She shuddered all over and stared at me for a second. She turned horribly pale, white as a sheet in fact, and then all at once, not impetuously but softly and gently, she bowed down to my feet. It wasn’t a boarding-school curtsey but a Russian bow, forehead to the floor. Then she jumped up and ran off. I was wearing my sword. I drew it and nearly stabbed myself with it on the spot. Why, I don’t know. It would have been frightfully stupid, of course. I suppose it was out of delight. Can you understand killing yourself out of delight? But I didn’t stab myself. I only kissed my sword and put it back in its scabbard—which I needn’t have told you, by the way. And I imagine that in telling you about my inner struggle I’ve laid it on rather thick, to glorify myself. But let it go, and to hell with everyone who pries into the human heart! Well, so much for that ‘adventure’ with Katerina Ivanovna. So now Ivan knows about it, and you—no one else.”

Dmitri stood up and took a step or two in his excitement. He pulled out his handkerchief and wiped his forehead, then sat down again, not where he’d sat before but on the opposite side, so that Alyosha had to turn all the way round to face him.
